question:
What is the value of the product of the \(9\) factors below?

\[ \begin{aligned} &\left(1 - \tfrac12\right)\left(1 - \tfrac13\right)\left(1 - \tfrac14\right) \cdots \\ &\quad {}\cdot \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{10}\right) \end{aligned} \]
solution:
Subtracting each unit fraction from \(1\) gives a numerator one less than its denominator. For example, \(1-\frac13=\frac23\). Thus the nine factors become
\[
\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac34\cdots\frac9{10}
=\frac{1\cdot2\cdots9}{2\cdot3\cdots10}.
\]
Every integer from \(2\) through \(9\) appears once in both the numerator and denominator. Canceling these nonzero factors leaves \(\frac1{10}\), choice \(\mathrm{A}\).

edges.reason: Adding equal-denominator parts uses the meaning of one such unit fraction and a count of equally sized parts.

The criteria expressly find common factors and reduce until numerator and denominator are coprime. These are the common-factor contents of the endpoint; finding the greatest factor in a single step is only a shortcut and is outside this required scope.
edges.scope: Finding a shared divisor and recognizing the absence of a shared divisor above one when reducing to simplest form

edges.reason: Reduction replaces numerator and denominator by division by the same common factor, using the value-preserving fraction property.
edges.scope: dividing numerator and denominator by a common number

edges.reason: The integer-multiplier case supplies a useful stepping stone and repeated-addition interpretation. The product-of-numerators/product-of-denominators rule follows directly from a part-of-a-part area model without executing the earlier decimal-free integer-multiplier procedure; Gemini confuses this customary progression with necessity.
Rational arithmetic helps evaluate surviving endpoint terms in fraction examples. The cancellation idea is structural and applies to symbolic, radical or other terms.
